title: Ψύλλα καὶ ἄνθρωπος
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 357. Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ψύλλα δέ ποτέ τινι πολλὰ ἠνώχλει.
sentences.tr: Psylla de pote tini polla ēnōchlei.
sentences.l: And a flea once was troubling a certain man greatly.
sentences.n: The fable opens with δέ, a connective looking back to the flea fable printed just before it: Chambry sets the three flea pieces down as a run, and this one begins as though mid-conversation. ἐνοχλέω takes the dative of the person troubled; πολλά is an adverbial accusative, 'much'.

sentences.t:
Καὶ δὴ συλλαβών· « Τίς εἶ σύ, ἀνεβόα,
ὅτι πάντα μου μέλη κατεβοσκήσω
εἰκῆ καὶ μάτην ἐμὲ καταναλίσκων ; »
sentences.tr:
Kai dē syllabōn· « Tis ei sy, aneboa,
hoti panta mou melē kateboskēsō
eikē kai matēn eme katanaliskōn ; »
sentences.l: And so, having caught her: « Who are you, » he was shouting, « that you have grazed over all my limbs, using me up idly and to no purpose? »
sentences.i: So he caught her and shouted: « Who are you, to have grazed over every limb of me, wasting me at random and for nothing? »
sentences.n: The sentence has no main verb outside the quotation: συλλαβών hangs on ἀνεβόα, which sits inside the speech as a parenthesis. καταβόσκομαι is used of cattle eating a field bare — the man's body is the pasture. ὅτι here gives the ground of the question, 'seeing that'. καταναλίσκων is masculine where the flea is feminine; the printed form is kept, and the slip may be the text's own or may show the writer thinking of the pest generically.

sentences.t:
Ἡ δὲ ἐβόα· « Οὕτως ζῶμεν, μὴ κτείνῃς·
μέγα γὰρ κακὸν οὐ δύναμαι ποιῆσαι. »
sentences.tr:
Hē de eboa· « Houtōs zōmen, mē kteinēis·
mega gar kakon ou dynamai poiēsai. »
sentences.l: And she cried: « This is how we live; do not kill me; for I cannot do any great harm. »
sentences.n: μή with the aorist subjunctive (κτείνῃς) is the regular way to forbid a single act, where μή with the present imperative forbids a practice. οὕτως ζῶμεν, 'so we live', pleads the flea's nature as her whole defence: it is not malice, it is her livelihood.

sentences.t:
Ὁ δὲ γελάσας πρὸς αὐτὴν οὕτως ἔφη·
« Ἄρτι τεθνήξῃ χερσί μου ταῖς ἰδίαις·
ἅπαν γὰρ κακόν, οὐ μικρόν, οὐδὲ μέγα
οὐδ’ ὅλως πρέπει καθόλου που φυῆναι.
sentences.tr:
Ho de gelasas pros autēn houtōs ephē·
« Arti tethnēxēi chersi mou tais idiais·
hapan gar kakon, ou mikron, oude mega
oud’ holōs prepei katholou pou phyēnai.
sentences.l: And he, laughing, spoke to her thus: « This instant you shall be dead by my own hands; for every evil, not the small one, nor the great, is in no way fitting to come into being at all, anywhere.
sentences.i: And he laughed and said to her: « You shall be dead this instant by my own hands; for no evil whatever, small or great, ought ever to come into being at all.
sentences.n: τεθνήξῃ is a future perfect doing the work of a plain future — θνῄσκω is one of the very few verbs that keep the form in use, and it says not 'you will die' but 'you will be dead'. The heaped negatives οὐ … οὐδέ … οὐδ’ ὅλως do not cancel one another; in Greek they pile up and strengthen. Chambry prints no closing guillemet on this speech, and none is added here.

sentences.t: Ὁ μῦθος δηλοῖ ὅτι ὁ κακὸς οὐ πρέπει ἐλεηθῆναι, κἂν μέγας ᾖ, κἂν μικρός.
sentences.tr: Ho mythos dēloi hoti ho kakos ou prepei eleēthēnai, kan megas ēi, kan mikros.
sentences.l: The fable shows that the bad man ought not to be pitied, even if he be great, even if small.
sentences.n: κἄν is καὶ ἐάν by crasis, twice over, the subjunctive ᾖ written once and carried across to the second clause. πρέπει is normally impersonal, 'it is fitting', with a dative and an infinitive; here ὁ κακός stands as its subject outright — a looseness this late prose allows.
